\smallskip
\noindent\footnotesize Notes: base x02's 0/7 aggregates s42, s1234, and the 5-seed sweep 777--781
(all neutral:100); v1 was re-judged at 8 frames (its 4-frame verdicts differ on x07). Bold = success
(target or synonym); $\dagger$ targets are never emitted by the judge (untestable).

All verdicts are Qwen2-VL-7B (do\_sample=False) over a fixed 15-class emotion taxonomy with a
confidence score; a cell is bold when the judged emotion equals the task target (joyful/cheerful
count via their in-taxonomy synonym \emph{happy}). ``f4/f8'' is the number of judge frames;
``s42/s1234/s999'' the sampling seed; ``8s/16s'' the inference steps. Empty (--) cells are
configurations that were not run. The judge never emits 11 of its 15 classes (incl.\ all of
worried/relieved/angry) across the whole re-judgment, so those targets are untestable with this
judge. Full raw logs and the 12-class released protocol are in the supplemental material.

\smallskip
\noindent\footnotesize Four-judge cross-check (round-21): the decisive x02 cell and its base control
were re-judged by three additional open VLMs under the identical 15-class protocol and frames
(Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-32B, Qwen3.8-27B). v3 x02 is sad under Qwen2-VL and Qwen3.8-27B (sad:80 and
sad:82/85, with explicit visual reasoning) and non-sad under Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL-32B
(neutral:85, worried:85); base x02 is neutral under all four (Table~\ref{tab:judges} in the paper).
All four judges fail the known-emotion validity check (1/17, 0/17, 1/17, 0/17 strict on the shared
17-portrait set; 4/17, 5/17, 6/17, 7/17 lenient per the paper's synonym rule) and none recognizes any
negative emotion (0/5). Raw verdicts and the derivation script \texttt{verify\_judge\_counts.py} are
in the released judge logs.

\smallskip
\noindent\footnotesize Full-matrix agreement: all 88 clip-configs above were additionally judged by
Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-32B and Qwen3.8-27B under the identical protocol
(\texttt{judge\_all88\_*.jsonl}, script \texttt{analyze\_agreement88.py}). Pairwise agreement is high
within a capability tier---71.6\% for the two 7B models (Cohen $\kappa{=}0.49$) and 68.8\% for the two
newest ($\kappa{=}0.63$)---and 41.6--47.7\% across tiers; 23 of the 77 configs covered by all four are
unanimous (Fleiss $\kappa{=}0.38$, or 33/77 and 0.48 under the synonym rule). Judges differ in
expressivity (classes used: 4/15, 6/15, 9/15, 9/15), and the disagreement is about \emph{whether} an
emotion is present: on the four-judge 77-config intersection, excluding configs both judges call neutral
leaves 36.7--50.0\% agreement, while on configs where both commit to a non-neutral emotion they agree
87.9--100\% (the corresponding figures on the three-judge 88-config set, quoted in the main text, are
33.8--45.7\% and 88--95\%).
\emph{Retraction note:} an earlier version of this appendix reported that the judges disagree on the
\emph{direction} of the intervention effect ($+7.0$/$-2.9$/$-8.1$pp). Those aggregates pooled a
heterogeneous configuration set in which base covers only 4 of the 8 transfer tasks at 16 steps, so the
arms were not task-matched and the reversal was an artifact of denominator composition (all three deltas
were also null, Fisher $p{\approx}0.42$--$0.50$). On the task-matched comparison no judge scores base
above v3; two of four score them equal.
\emph{Option-order control:} reversing the order of the 15 answer options---same judge, same frames,
greedy decoding---changes 17/88 verdicts for Qwen2-VL (self-agreement 80.7\%, $\kappa{=}0.65$) and
10/88 for Qwen3-VL-32B (88.6\%, $\kappa{=}0.86$), while a duplicate run of the identical configuration
reproduces 88/88 labels (\texttt{judge\_all88\_*\_rev.jsonl}).
\emph{Frame-span control:} the 8 judged frames above span only the first second of each 5.2\,s,
124-frame clip. Re-extracting 8 frames across the whole clip (\texttt{extract8\_full.py}) and changing
nothing else moves 32/97 verdicts for Qwen2-VL (self-agreement 67.0\%, $\kappa{=}0.48$), 32/97 for
Qwen2.5-VL (67.0\%) and 34/97 for Qwen3-VL-32B (64.9\%, $\kappa{=}0.57$), predominantly
neutral$\rightarrow$committed (28 of Qwen2-VL's 32); target-hit rates rise on both arms---base
8/34$\rightarrow$16/34 (exact McNemar $p{=}0.021$), LoRA 13/63$\rightarrow$23/63 and
20/63$\rightarrow$33/63 ($p{=}0.002$, $0.001$), with no LoRA-arm change under Qwen2.5-VL
(17/63$\rightarrow$18/63). Base x02 judged sad rises 0/8$\rightarrow$3/8, 0/8$\rightarrow$2/8 and
2/8$\rightarrow$3/8, so the ``base is never sad'' control does not hold; the task-level claim is retracted
in the main text on the strength of the paired 8-task matrix (base 4/16, 6/16, 9/16 vs v3 6/16, 6/16,
8/16; Fisher $p{\ge}0.70$). Logs: \texttt{judge\_full\_q2.jsonl}, \texttt{judge\_full\_q3vl.jsonl}; script
\texttt{analyze\_framespan.py}. Both frame sets are verifiably from the same videos (the full-span f01
is byte-identical to the original f05, $t{\approx}0.72$\,s).

\emph{Is full-clip scoring better or merely different?} With no human labels the only available validity
signal is reliability: if independent judges agree more on the same clips, the longer window measures the
intended quantity more consistently. Over the 97 clips scored under both protocols, all three judge pairs
move the same way but only one significantly: Qwen2-VL vs Qwen3-VL-32B agrees 50.5\% ($\kappa{=}0.348$) at
0--1\,s and 56.7\% ($\kappa{=}0.462$) over the full clip ($\Delta\kappa{=}{+}0.114$; paired bootstrap over
clips, $B{=}20000$, seed 7, $P(\Delta\kappa{\le}0){=}0.035$), while Qwen2-VL vs Qwen2.5-VL gives
$+0.011$ and Qwen2.5-VL vs Qwen3-VL-32B $+0.001$. Full-clip scoring is therefore not \emph{less} reliable
and plausibly more so, but we do not claim it is systematically more reliable, and reliability is not
correctness, which needs human labels
(\texttt{reliability()} in \texttt{analyze\_framespan.py}; the all-pairs version is
\texttt{reliability\_all\_pairs()} in \texttt{analyze\_basefull.py}).

\emph{Task-matched base matrix (round 9):} the base model was regenerated on all 8 transfer tasks at both
seeds (16 steps, 768$^2$, 124 frames, \texttt{run\_basefull4.sh}; 16/16 clips produced) and judged with the
same 15-class protocol, giving 16 fully paired cells per judge. Base vs v3: 4/16 vs 6/16 (Qwen2-VL, Fisher
$p{=}0.704$, exact McNemar $p{=}0.688$), 6/16 vs 6/16 (Qwen2.5-VL, $p{=}1.000$ both), 9/16 vs 8/16
(Qwen3-VL-32B, $p{=}1.000$ both) and 8/12 vs 8/12 (Qwen3.8-27B, $p{=}1.000$ both; it parses 12 of the 16
cells). Two cells falsify earlier premises under the primary protocol: base x02
at seed 42 is judged \emph{sad} by Qwen3-VL-32B and base x08 at seed 1234 \emph{angry} by Qwen2-VL and
Qwen3-VL-32B. Logs \texttt{judge\_basefull\_\{q2,q25,q3vl\}.jsonl}, script \texttt{analyze\_basefull.py}.
Logs \texttt{judge\_basefull\_q38.jsonl} for the fourth judge; it runs at minutes per clip in plain
\texttt{transformers} (it emits a long deliberation before its \texttt{WORD:SCORE} line), so only the
16-cell 0--1\,s pass was run with it and no full-span number depends on it.

Strict hits rise 0/14$\rightarrow$3/14, 0/14$\rightarrow$4/14 and 5/14$\rightarrow$9/14; leniently
4/14$\rightarrow$8/14, 3/14$\rightarrow$9/14 ($p{=}0.031$) and 7/14$\rightarrow$11/14. Across the six
comparisons 25 clip verdicts change correctness and \emph{all 25} favour the whole clip, none the opening.
The labels are the batch's intended expressions, not our annotation of these clips, and emotions no judge
can emit (anxious, curious, relaxed) fail under both protocols. Script
\texttt{analyze\_gt\_accuracy.py}, logs \texttt{judge\_gt\{1s,full\}\_\{q2,q25,q3vl\}.jsonl},
generation driver \texttt{run\_gt.sh}.
